**Use append-only JSONL.**

## Why

**The volume is negligible.** ~100 lines/week is ~5,200 lines/year. Even at 1 KB per record that's ~5 MB/year — a file `grep`, `jq`, and Python all read end-to-end in milliseconds. SQLite's core advantages (indexed lookup, not loading everything into memory) don't activate at this scale. You'd be paying setup cost for a benefit that never arrives.

**Single-threaded, one machine removes SQLite's other main advantage.** SQLite earns its keep with concurrent writers, transactional multi-table updates, and crash-safe partial writes. You have one writer, one process, one append per run. `open(path, 'a')` + one `write()` of a line ending in `\n` is atomic enough in practice for records under the pipe buffer size, and a torn final line is trivially detectable and discardable on read.

**Humans read the records.** This is the deciding factor. A JSONL file is readable with `tail`, `less`, `grep`, and `jq` — no client, no schema knowledge, no `.mode json`. A reviewer on a machine without your tooling can still read it. A SQLite file is opaque without the CLI, doesn't diff, doesn't render in a code host, and can't be pasted into a review comment.

**Schema evolution is free.** Eval harnesses grow fields constantly — new metric, new model ID, new config knob. JSONL absorbs a new key with zero ceremony; old rows just lack it. SQLite makes you write `ALTER TABLE` migrations, and forces you to decide *now* what the columns are, which you don't yet know.

**It composes with the tools you already have.** Git-appendable (line-oriented, clean diffs, meaningful blame), `cat`-concatenable across machines, streamable to any downstream analysis. Whatever ad-hoc question you get during review, one `jq` line answers it.

## What you give up, honestly

- **No indexed queries.** Fine at 5k rows; a full scan is instant. If you ever want SQL, `jq -c | sqlite3 :memory:` loads the whole ledger into a temp DB on demand. The JSONL stays the source of truth; SQLite becomes a derived view you rebuild whenever you want it.
- **No enforced schema.** Compensate with a validator — a `RunRecord` dataclass or Pydantic model serialized on write. That gives you the write-side guarantee SQLite's schema would, without the read-side rigidity.
- **No in-place updates.** This is a feature. Run records are immutable facts. If you need to annotate one, append a correction record referencing the original run ID rather than mutating history.

## Practical shape

One record per run, one line, stable field order (sort keys) so diffs are clean. Include a `schema_version`, a ULID/UUID run ID, and an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp as the first fields — it makes lines self-describing and sorts chronologically. Rotate by period if it ever grows (`runs-2026-Q3.jsonl`), though at your rate a single file lasts years.

## When to revisit

Switch to SQLite if any of these become true: concurrent writers appear (parallel eval workers), you need frequent point lookups over hundreds of thousands of rows, or you start maintaining relational structure across multiple record types with referential integrity. None of those are on your horizon. Until then, SQLite is a heavier tool solving problems you don't have, at the cost of the one property you actually need — that a human can read the file.
